title: Herpetological misinformation and sensationalism: media framing on biological and ecological aspects of the golden lancehead (Bothrops insularis)
screen_reason: Content analysis of 230 online sources (Google News articles and YouTube videos in English, Portuguese and Spanish, published May 2013 - April 2025) about the golden lancehead and Queimada Grande Island, each screened in full against the scientific literature for factually incorrect statements across 17 defined topics. 94.35% (n=217) contained misinformation - a quantitative falsity share of items with a stated denominator (CONTENT). Sensationalist language (83.91%) is an editorial-tone measure and is recorded as QUALITY.

estimates.country: Not stated for the sources (media in English, Portuguese and Spanish about a Brazilian island; searches run in all three languages)
estimates.platform: Google News articles and YouTube videos
estimates.date: Content published online May 2013 to April 2025; searches and coding carried out for that window (paper published 2026)
estimates.measure_type: % of online sources (news articles and YouTube videos) about Bothrops insularis / Queimada Grande Island that contained misinformation
estimates.value_raw: From these sources, 94.35% (n=217) contained misinformation [of 230 sources]
estimates.denominator: 230 online sources containing information about B. insularis and Queimada Grande Island (69 in English, 77 in Portuguese, 84 in Spanish; 62 Google News articles and 168 YouTube videos), retrieved with Boolean species/island searches in three languages, published May 2013 - April 2025, with replicates across languages
estimates.definition: the source contained at least one statement judged incorrect or outdated (or lacking accuracy) against current reliable scientific sources, in any of 17 coded topics (venom, antivenom, population density, species image, other species, island info, island image, prey, habit, morphology, defense, predators, activity, origin, threats, market value, reproduction)
estimates.misinfo_def: "In this paper, false and inaccurate information is referred to as misinformation, which is the inadvertent spread of false information without intent to harm (Shu et al. 2020). ... The judgement on the information provided in such contents as either incorrect or outdated, including information that lacks a certain level of accuracy, was based on current and reliable scientific sources."
estimates.n: 230 online sources (news articles and YouTube videos)
estimates.source_quote: From these sources, 94.35% (n=217) contained misinformation, and 83.91% (n=193) used sensationalist language in their content.
estimates.page_loc: p. 7, Results, 'Data collection'; Tables I and II
estimates.ground_truth_detail: The three herpetologist authors read every article and watched every video in full and judged statements against current scientific literature, supported by an in-paper literature review of the species' natural history; per-topic misinformation definitions with worked examples are given in the Methods. Number of independent coders per item and any inter-coder reliability are not reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: To survey the information disseminated by digital media about B. insularis and Queimada Grande Island, we searched Google News articles and YouTube for videos, using the following Boolean operators in English, Portuguese, and Spanish ... Only content published online from May 2013 to April 2025 was included in the analysis. All Google News articles and YouTube videos related to B. insularis and Queimada Grande Island were screened for the presence of misinformation and sensationalist content.
estimates.notes: Single-species keyword corpus, so denom_scope=topical and denom_selection is blank (all retrieved items were screened, not a top-N slice). platform_norm=multi_platform because the denominator mixes Google News articles (n=62) and YouTube videos (n=168); the paper never reports a per-platform total, only platform x language cells (see missed_or_uncertain), and summing those would be a forbidden cross-category sum. breadth coded 'false' (the numerator is factually incorrect claims, e.g. venom potency, population density); note the rubric also admits 'outdated' and 'lacks a certain level of accuracy' content, so 'misleading' is a defensible alternative. year=2025 is the end of the publication window and the search year; the corpus spans 2013-2025, so this is not a single-year snapshot. Country is Global/unspecified: the media are multinational (US, UK, Indian, Brazilian, Spanish-language outlets) even though the subject matter is Brazilian.

estimates.definition: the source contained emotionally charged / sensational terms such as 'deadliest', 'most venomous', 'melt human flesh'
estimates.misinfo_def: "Sensationalism (also called malinformation) is a type of editorial bias in mass media that includes over-hyped topics in order to attract more audiences (Udeze & Uzuegbunam 2013). ... we classified as sensationalist any sources containing sensational terms such as 'deadliest', 'most venomous', and 'melt human flesh'."
estimates.source_quote: From these sources, 94.35% (n=217) contained misinformation, and 83.91% (n=193) used sensationalist language in their content.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Authors' coding of emotionally charged vocabulary, following Nanni et al. (2020); no reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Thus, we classified as sensationalist any sources containing sensational terms such as "deadliest", "most venomous", and "melt human flesh".
estimates.notes: Coded QUALITY (excluded from prevalence) and borderline=true: sensationalism is an editorial-tone judgement - a wholly accurate article could be labelled sensationalist for using words like 'deadliest' - so it fails the CONTENT test of an external truth/falsity standard. Kept because it is one of the paper's two headline numbers and because the review may want tone measures separated from falsity measures.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Platform x language cells were not written as separate rows (the overall 94.35% is the paper's headline and the language sets contain 'many replicates', so splitting risks double counting): news articles - Portuguese 24/29 (82.76%), English 16/16 (100%), Spanish 17/17 (100%); YouTube videos - English 52/53 (98.11%), Portuguese 43/48 (89.6%), Spanish 65/67 (97.01%). A per-platform total (all news articles vs all YouTube videos) is not reported and could only be obtained by summing across languages, which R8 forbids. An adjudicator wanting a platform moderator should use these six verbatim cells. (2) Sensationalism by platform x language: news articles 87.5% English, 48.28% Portuguese, 100% Spanish; YouTube 96.23% English, 64.58% Portuguese, 95.52% Spanish. (3) Topic-level misinformation frequencies are sub-numerators within each platform x language cell (e.g. English news: venom 93.75%, photos 50%, density and morphology 37.5% each; English YouTube: venom 94.34%, density 64.15%, species image 58.49%; Spanish YouTube: venom 85.08%, density 76.12%, species image 74.63%; Portuguese YouTube: venom 83.33%, density 54.17%, island info 43.75%; Portuguese news: venom 62.06%, density 48.27%, habits/diet 41.37%; Spanish news: density 82.35%, venom 70.58%, island info and other species 52.94% each) and would double-count against the main row. (4) Expert-consultation figures: 3/16 (18.75%) English news articles and 11/53 (20.76%) English YouTube videos mentioned an expert and all still contained misinformation; 12/29 (41.38%) Portuguese articles and 25% of Portuguese videos mentioned an expert, of which 66.67% and 83.33% respectively contained misinformation; only 1/65 (1.54%) Spanish videos mentioned an expert. These are conditional (within-expert-mention) falsity shares, i.e. a moderator analysis rather than the paper's prevalence estimate, so no rows were written; the 66.67% and 83.33% figures are the most extractable of them if an adjudicator wants them. (5) View counts (YouTube total 198,480,355 views; English mean 2,998,019) are reach indicators but no share of views was attributed to misinformation, so no EXPOSURE row is possible. (6) The abstract's rounded 'approximately 94%' and the discussion's 'nearly 95%' / 'almost 84%' restate the same two values; the precise Results figures were used. (7) The 60% trafficking figure and the venom-mortality percentages are cited clinical/enforcement statistics, not study results.

rob.design: Census-style keyword survey of Google News and YouTube in three languages (Boolean strings given in full) for content published May 2013 - April 2025; 230 sources retrieved (69 English, 77 Portuguese, 84 Spanish; 62 news articles, 168 videos), with acknowledged replication across languages and no probability sampling. Every article was read and every video watched in full by the authors (herpetologists), coding misinformation across 17 pre-defined topics with worked examples and an in-paper natural-history literature review as the standard, plus a sensationalism (emotive-language) code and an expert-consultation code. Weaknesses: no inter-coder reliability or double coding reported, no pre-registration, ground truth is the authors' own expert judgement, search-engine result sets are personalised and not reproducible, view counts unavailable for news articles, and the misinformation definition admits outdated or imprecise content alongside outright false claims.
